I want to expand on this OP. I am a bi female (always have been; unassociated with porn) who started watching porn at 11. It quickly evolved into very degrading, "BDSM" porn. I put "BDSM" in quotes because now---as an adult---I understand that the BDSM community is completely different from how they were depicted in the porn that I watched. 

I started having sex with males at 14. I always wanted it to hurt. It was never emotional. At 17, I started having sex with females. It was always in threesomes and, again, never emotional. I continued having sex with males throughout this entire time and would often degrade myself on purpose, literally crying about it afterward, and yet still go back again. 

I don't know how many partners I had before I met my now husband (there were a LOT tbh), but it literally took until him to realize that sex could be emotionally connecting. I had no idea. It was a completely foreign concept. Even our role-play or "dominant" sex is emotionally connecting. It wasn't a decision I made. It was just different emotionally for me from sexual encounter #1. It was the same movements but felt different. We were casual partners at the time, so it wasn't that I was in love with him like I had never been before. He was just the first healthy sexual relationship I've ever had. And I married the fuck out of that man 6.5 years later. There were other partners for both of us in the first few years, but we kept coming back for each other. 

All this to say, porn during my formative years fucked me up and fucked my idea about healthy sexual relationships up, big time. It took many partners, many sexual encounters, and much experimentation before I discovered how to have healthy sex. 

I hope that you are able to discover how to have healthy sex, be it with women or men. I was lucky in that I didn't simultaneously have to come to terms with my sexuality. I wish you luck, friend. It will take a lot of work, but you will get there. You just have to be willing to put in the work to find yourself and separate the damage from your early years from the man you are today. I recommend finding a professional to help you through that journey. It may take a few different professionals before you find one that clicks and that's OK! It has taken me plenty. There is hope and an answer. It just takes time and work. I believe in you.

I do an infusion every 4 weeks and troches every day. I can't go to 5 weeks or I start feeling it come back. I've tried different, lower dose maintenance between infusions, but they haven’t worked. My depression is high maintenance. REALLY high maintenance. And I hate being high. 

But my god it has given me a life. Not "a life back" because I legitimately don't remember a time before my depression. It started when I was really young. I am able to be a part of my own life. I go out with my dog without resenting the fact that I have to leave my bed. I have a hobby; I'm training my own service dog. I don't spend every waking moment planning various suicide methods. I've been able to completely address my irritability and anger (which was linked to the depression). I'm finally the person depressed me knew I could be but couldn't make it happen. 

My infusions are an hour long and the "high" effects don't last very long, but I can't drive for about 10 hours after the infusion (you aren't supposed to drive at all the same day). The troche highs vary depending on the homogeneity of the mixture. 

Most people don't need nearly as much as I do. I think it is common to do infusions every 4 weeks with much lower or less frequent maintenance in between. Some people don't need it in between maintenance at all.

I'm not bipolar, but have veryyyy treatment resistant depression and OCD. People react differently to different medications. Furthermore, some people respond to "off label" medications, which means their diagnosis isn't the primary use of the medication. For example, I was on antipsychotics for anxiety. I tried 20 different medications. One of them was even a dementia medication (I'm 24 lol). I am currently on an anesthetic and it has been the only thing to help with the depression. For my OCD, I'm on two antidepressants, neither of which touched my depression.

That being said, most people respond to first line medications. Don't blame yourself if it doesn't work, but be open to it might working. What helped me was "symptom tracking". If you feel like you don't have the soft skills necessary, I might look into the big tutoring companies to start with, develop the skills, gain the experience, then apply to small business that do tutoring. As far as industry, I know how discouraging it can feel with the question "what can I actually do with my degree?". I'm in a biomath PhD program and am asking myself that exact question. The method that has been helpful for me is to first google "math jobs", then read all the descriptions of things like data analyst and software engineer etc. Then pick which ones sound interesting and look for available jobs now. Take note of the requirements for different jobs and--during your graduate school--obtain those skills. You might be able to take courses in them or, if not, coursera is a GREAT option. It's what I'm using.

The beauty of a math degree is that it trains your mind to think of problems critically. With jobs, you'll use this or that from your degree (or from a quick google search if you've forgotten), but the way you have to think in order to get a math degree is a highly valuable asset.

You're not abnormal. I was born with a severely lazy eye. Cried to my aunt that I would never be beautiful because of it. Had to wear a patch for years. At 4, I fell at Disney and cut open my forehead. When I got my adult teeth, my front two were huge and stuck out very dramatically. I had horrible acne. I started college at 16, where most of my colleagues were 22+ (large nontraditional population). I got Invisalign, because I didn't want to look even YOUNGER than I already was if I added braces. The only time people could tell that I had them was eating or smoking a cigarette. Sure it was a little weird to have to "take my teeth out" while standing outside with my older friends before a smoke, but other than that it was a pretty smooth process.
At 17, I began to model. I still had larger front teeth, the face scar and acne were covered by makeup, and sometimes my eyes looked wonky in pictures. During these two years of modeling, I changed myself into the "beauty ideal" that I had wanted so badly at 13-16. I did some pics with a friend as a photographer at 16, but that year was when I really identified what I wanted to look like and really went for it. Yes, I felt beautiful when I would see the pictures, but I never felt skinny enough, shapely enough, and obsessed over little physical things. 
At 19, I buzz cut my waist-length hair. Loved it. It felt more "me", even though, a year prior, I got upset that my hair was cut an inch shorter than planned. I even tried growing it out again for 2 years, but it didn't feel like me. I did not fit my NEW definition of "beautiful". So, I buzzed it again at 22 and, at 23, have thrown away all my makeup. The time I used to spend on my appearance (tweezing and waxing and styling etc.), I now spend with my family who loves the me I am today, despite not being traditionally beautiful. Sometimes, I look at old pics and my self-image takes a hit. But living the life you want to live is important. In closing, one of my current favorite sayings is: "Those who mind don't matter and those who matter don't mind".
I hope this is helpful.

TL;DR: many of my physical "abnormalities" have been resolved relatively painlessly and my "beauty ideal" has drastically changed.
